summary.text: Irene’s published Orthodox lives recount conversion, public preaching, prolonged suffering, and many conversions. The stories honor her as a Great Martyr, while their descriptions of her final departure differ.

blocks.text: The OCA calls her Penelope, daughter of Licinius and Licinia. Her Christian tutor Apellian teaches her; Timothy baptizes her with the name Irene. She rejects a proposed marriage and destroys her father’s idols.
blocks.reason: Necessary concise account of the named modern ecclesiastical life; permission for full reproduction has not been established. Traditional events and miracle narratives remain attributed to that publication.

blocks.text: Her father’s attempt to have horses trample her ends in his death and restoration through her prayer. Further rulers persecute her; the narrative describes preaching, imprisonment, miraculous preservation, and numerous baptisms.

blocks.title: Mark 9:23–24
blocks.text:
Jesus said unto him, If thou canst believe, all things are possible to him that believeth.

And straightway the father of the child cried out, and said with tears, Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief.

The longer OCA account follows successive confrontations rather than one uninterrupted trial. It names several cities and rulers and describes repeated preservation from torture. Its episodes include the pit of serpents and heated bronze oxen. These belong to the transmitted martyr narrative; their place in the story is retained without presenting them as independently verified judicial records.

blocks.text: The OCA relates a beheading followed by restoration to life, then an empty tomb near Ephesus. It explicitly reports conflicting final traditions: death by fire in Western martyrologies and beheading in Basil II’s Menologion.
blocks.reason: Necessary concise account of the named modern ecclesiastical life; permission for full reproduction has not been established. Traditional events and miracle narratives remain attributed to that publication.

blocks.text: The GOARCH reading instead ends with peaceful repose at Ephesus in the first half of the fourth century. Two days later the grave is found open and empty. The martyr title therefore does not establish one uncontested final death method.
blocks.reason: Necessary concise account of the named modern ecclesiastical life; permission for full reproduction has not been established. Traditional events and miracle narratives remain attributed to that publication.

blocks.text: The same Greek account remembers churches dedicated to Irene at Constantinople and her patronage of Thera. It connects the island’s common name Santorini with Saint Irene. Its concise narrative stresses steadfast faith through repeated sufferings and journeys. These are reported features of the published life, rather than independently documented travel or casualty records.
blocks.reason: Necessary concise account of the named modern ecclesiastical life; permission for full reproduction has not been established. Traditional events and miracle narratives remain attributed to that publication.

blocks.text: The shorter GOARCH reading preserves the same central identity—Licinius’s daughter Penelope, renamed Irene at baptism—while abbreviating her journeys. It includes her father’s conversion after restoration to life and connects her preaching with numerous conversions. Its account is useful alongside the longer OCA life because readers can see both common narrative elements and different endings. The commemoration remains May 5 in the printed sources. No calculated modern civil date, reconstructed itinerary, or single harmonized death method is substituted for what those sources actually say.
